hippo-t2c-em-Q1.html:
From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). Shock is tissue hypoperfusion, not a blood pressure number: this man has tachycardia, cool extremities, cap refill 4 s and oliguria (no void in 12 h), and the lecture's class table keeps BP normal through class II losses, so A fails. The deficit is ECF volume from GI losses, so replace it with an isotonic crystalloid that stays in the ECF.

  • E: Ringer's lactate stays in the ECF (13 - IV Fluids, PoM 1 GU) - the right volume expander.
  • B: D5W is free water, distributing 2/3 into the ICF, so it barely expands plasma.
  • C: 0.5 mL/kg/h is the oliguria threshold / minimum resuscitation target rather than a 'normal' output (see flag).
  • D: sat is 99% on room air; oxygen is not the critical intervention here.

flags.title: Option C is arguably true
flags.html: Many references quote 0.5 mL/kg/h as the lower limit of adequate adult urine output, so C can be read as a true statement. It is best read as the oliguria cut-off rather than a normal value, which is presumably why the key prefers E; the vault notes do not give this number.

hippo-t2c-em-Q10:
From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). The lethal triad is acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy, and each distractor is a named countermeasure to one arm of it:

  • A warmed products via a rapid transfuser (Level I warmer) - prevents hypothermia.
  • B, D platelets and plasma - offset the dilutional coagulopathy that worsens progressively at 10, 20, 30 units of pRBC.
  • E serial blood gases - track the acidosis that cripples Ca-dependent clotting complexes (rFVIIa activity falls 90% at pH 7.0).
  • C intubation may well be needed in a massive variceal bleed for airway protection, but that is an airway indication, not a measure against the triad - hence the answer.
hippo-t2c-em-Q11:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis (FoM Block 4, Week 14). Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection, and the lecture lists the bedside signs: confusion (brain), tachypnea (lung), hypotension and tachycardia. A febrile patient with abdominal pain has a presumed infection, and she already shows altered mentation, RR 24 and SBP 84 - all three qSOFA items - so A is right.

  • B: a normal WBC does not exclude sepsis; the definition rests on organ dysfunction, not leukocytosis.
  • C, E: recognition is clinical and must not wait - every hour of antibiotic delay after hypotension adds about 8% mortality.
  • D: MAP is about 70 here, but a MAP above 65 does not exclude sepsis; MAP 65 is the septic-shock vasopressor target, not a sepsis criterion.
hippo-t2c-em-Q12:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis (FoM Block 4, Week 14). The lecture defines sepsis (Sepsis-3) as life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response. This patient has a likely strep pharyngitis and every SIRS item (HR 122, RR 23, T 39.1, WBC 18), but no organ dysfunction: GCS normal, cap refill 2 s, BP 125/82, pH and lactate normal. Her tachycardia and fever are an appropriate, adaptive response to a local infection, so C is right.

  • A: SIRS criteria were dropped from the sepsis definition because they flag exactly this kind of healthy inflammatory response.
  • B: SBP is not the discriminator; organ dysfunction is.
  • D: a formal SOFA score is not needed at the bedside - the lecture notes it is mostly a trial tool - and the clinical picture already shows no failing organ.
  • E: a bacterial infection alone is not sepsis.
hippo-t2c-em-Q13:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis (FoM Block 4, Week 14). The lecture defines septic shock as hypotension that does not respond to fluids (arteriolar vasodilation plus capillary leak), which is why vasopressors are added. After a full 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus he is still 82/40 with lactate 3.5, so B is right; the Sepsis-3 definition adds the persistent lactate above 2.

  • A: an elevated lactate alone is hypoperfusion, not septic shock; it is the pairing with fluid-refractory hypotension that defines it.
  • C: hypothermia and leukopenia are markers of severe sepsis - the lecture lists hypothermia or fever - and they worsen the prognosis.
  • D: cultures are not required to diagnose or treat; antibiotics must not wait on them.
  • E: 30 mL/kg is the standard adequate initial bolus.

hippo-t2c-em-Q14.html:
From the VTE section of 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (FoM Block 3, Week 10). This is obstructive shock: hypotension, tachycardia, cool extremities and a distended JVP with clear, equal lungs. Active cancer scores on the Wells PE rule and lupus carries antiphospholipid antibodies, which the lecture ranks among the strongest thrombophilias (about 80x risk), so PE (E) is most likely.

  • A: CHF would give crackles, not clear lung fields.
  • B: no cough or fever and clear lungs.
  • C: lupus and cancer both cause effusions (03 - Pericardial Disease, PoM 1), but POCUS shows no effusion, which excludes tamponade.
  • D: tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds on one side; hers are equal and clear.

hippo-t2c-em-Q15.html:
From 03 - Pericardial Disease (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 2). The lecture lists radiation-induced injury among the traumatic/iatrogenic causes of pericarditis and effusion (and chest irradiation causes about 20% of constriction), so A is true.

  • B: pericardiocentesis is a needle into the pericardial space next to beating myocardium and coronaries; it carries real risk of laceration, arrhythmia and pneumothorax.
  • C: the reverse - the lecture's key point is that rate, not volume, decides tamponade: slow accumulation is tolerated up to 2 L, fast accumulation causes symptoms at 200-300 mL.
  • D: the lecture attributes electrical alternans to the heart swinging in the fluid, beat to beat (see flag).
  • E: it is done under echo (ultrasound) guidance at the bedside, not fluoroscopy.

flags.title: Option D is close to true
flags.html: 03 - Pericardial Disease explains electrical alternans as the heart swinging in the effusion, and some texts describe that motion as rotation of the heart. D is presumably wrong by its wording rather than its idea; do not over-learn the distinction.

hippo-t2c-em-Q16.html:
From the VTE section of 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (FoM Block 3, Week 10). In the lecture's PE column, CXR and ECG are there to find other causes (pneumonia, pneumothorax, MI) - they do not make the diagnosis, because in PE the chest x-ray is usually normal (D).

  • A: D-dimer is only for the unlikely group (Wells 4 or less); a negative excludes, a positive means nothing, so with high pretest probability go straight to CTPA.
  • B: a normal saturation does not exclude PE.
  • C: the commonest ECG finding is sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 is classic but uncommon.
  • E: the Wells PE items are cancer, surgery/bedrest, previous VTE, hemoptysis, HR over 100, PE most likely and DVT signs - the pill is not one.

flags.title: Partly beyond the vault notes
flags.html: The Wells items and the D-dimer rule come from the lecture; the ECG and saturation claims (B, C) are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

hippo-t2c-em-Q17.html:
From 04 - Myocardial Infarction and 05 - Complications of Acute MI (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 3). Hypotension, hypoperfusion and diffuse bilateral crackles is cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema (Killip class IV). The immediate threat is breathing: saturation 85% on a non-rebreather with RR 32 and accessory muscle use is failing oxygenation, and the lecture's pulmonary edema management includes BiPAP - with intubation for the patient too unstable for it. ABCs come first, so D.

  • A: a fluid bolus worsens pulmonary edema.
  • B: no fever or cough - no reason to lead with antibiotics.
  • C: pressors are likely needed, but only after the airway and breathing are secured.
  • E: furosemide treats the edema but will drop an already low BP and does not fix the hypoxia now.

hippo-t2c-em-Q18:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis (FoM Block 4, Week 14). Fever, malodorous lochia and lower abdominal pain five days after delivery is postpartum endometritis (the endometritis reference note: the most common postpartum infection), and HR 132, BP 92/48 and RR 22 make it sepsis with hypotension. With monitor and IVs in place, the next step is volume resuscitation (B), with broad-spectrum antibiotics alongside - the lecture's single most life-saving move, though not offered here.

  • A: saturation is 98% on room air.
  • C, E: packing and D&C address hemorrhage or retained products; three pads a day is not a postpartum hemorrhage.
  • D: imaging for a source comes after resuscitation has started.
hippo-t2c-em-Q19:
From the VTE section of 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (FoM Block 3, Week 10). Unilateral leg swelling, active cancer, dyspnea, tachycardia and hypotension with a normal CXR and no effusion is massive PE - obstructive shock. The lecture keeps thrombolysis for a small group: patients who may die in the next 24-48 h, accepting the much higher bleeding risk. A hypotensive PE is that patient, so A.

  • B: Wells is well over 4 (cancer, DVT signs, HR over 100, PE most likely), so D-dimer has no role - go to imaging.
  • C: no infection.
  • D: fluids cannot push past a mechanical obstruction; the clot must be treated.
  • E: needle decompression treats tension pneumothorax, which the normal CXR excludes.
hippo-t2c-em-Q2:
From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). The lecture lists the eight features of shock: hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria, abnormal mental status, tachypnea, cool clammy cyanotic skin, metabolic acidosis and hyperlactatemia. A lactate of 1.1 sits inside the normal range, so it is the one finding that does not point to hypoperfusion (C).

  • A mottled skin - the cool, cyanotic skin of poor perfusion.
  • B altered mental status - brain hypoperfusion (anxious to confused through the classes).
  • D, E tachypnea and tachycardia - both on the list, and tachycardia is the first vital to move.

A normal lactate does not exclude early shock; it simply is not evidence for it.
hippo-t2c-em-Q20:
From 06 - Hemorrhagic Shock (PoM 2 Repro, Week 6). After high-speed trauma, HR 132 and BP 72/40 is the lecture's class III-IV picture - tachycardia first, then falling BP once more than 30% of volume is lost - and hemorrhage is by far the commonest cause of shock in trauma (B).

  • A: neurogenic shock from cord injury removes sympathetic tone, giving hypotension with bradycardia or a normal HR, not 132.
  • C, D: tamponade and tension pneumothorax are real obstructive causes in trauma, but they need specific signs (distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, effusion) and are less common; assume bleeding until proven otherwise.
  • E: spinal shock is a temporary loss of cord reflexes below an injury - a neurological state, not a type of circulatory shock.

hippo-t2c-em-Q21.html:
Compressions do not restart the heart; they generate enough forward flow to keep the brain and heart perfused until a definitive therapy (defibrillation, reversal of the cause) can work. Survival that matters is survival with intact neurological function, so C.

  • A: ROSC is the goal of the whole resuscitation - shocks, drugs, treating Hs and Ts - not of CPR alone.
  • B: venous return during recoil is a mechanism of CPR, not its purpose.
  • D: finding the cause is a parallel task for the team.
  • E: it is active treatment, not a holding pattern.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

hippo-t2c-em-Q22.html: False. Survival to hospital discharge after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is roughly 1 in 10 in Canada and the US - about half of the 20% the statement claims. Survival is far higher for a witnessed arrest in a shockable rhythm with bystander CPR and early AED use, which is exactly why the chain of survival stresses early recognition, early CPR and early defibrillation.

flags.html: HippoNotes gives this true/false item with no answer at all, so the truth value above is reasoned, not transcribed from the bank.

hippo-t2c-em-Q23.html:
Adult BLS compressions have a fixed set of quality markers: rate 100-120/min, depth at least 2 inches (5-6 cm), full chest recoil between compressions, minimal interruptions, and a compression-to-ventilation ratio of 30:2 without an advanced airway. 15:1 matches no adult protocol (15:2 is two-rescuer paediatric CPR), so D is the exception.

  • A: 110-120 sits inside the 100-120 window, so it is acceptable (see flag).
  • B, C, E: recoil, few pauses and 2-inch depth are all core components.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

flags.title: Option A is worded oddly
flags.html: The guideline rate is 100-120/min; the bank's 110-120 is a narrower range inside it, so read A as correct rather than as a second exception.

hippo-t2c-em-Q24.html:
From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5), its cardiac arrest algorithm. The algorithm's core loop is continuous CPR with a shock for VF/pulseless VT, and the two interventions with the strongest link to neurologically intact survival are the earliest ones: early CPR and early defibrillation (B). Survival falls with every minute of delay to the first shock.

  • A, E: targeted temperature management is post-arrest care after ROSC - useful, but not the key determinant.
  • C: cardioversion is a synchronized shock for a rhythm with a pulse; it has no role in arrest.
  • D: epinephrine every 3-5 min is in the algorithm but improves ROSC more than neurologically good survival.

flags.title: Partly beyond the vault notes
flags.html: The algorithm is in the lecture; the claims about which steps drive neurological outcome (and TTM, epinephrine evidence) are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

hippo-t2c-em-Q25.html:
The adult out-of-hospital chain of survival runs: recognition and activation of the emergency response (call 911 / for help) → high-quality CPR → defibrillation → advanced resuscitation → post-arrest care → recovery. Calling for help is first because every later link (AED, EMS, advanced care) depends on it arriving, so D.

  • A, E: the second and third links.
  • B, C: the later, hospital- or EMS-level links.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

hippo-t2c-em-Q26.html:
From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5), its cardiac arrest algorithm. VT becomes a cardiac arrest rhythm the moment the pulse is lost: pulseless VT is shocked immediately, like VF, whereas VT with a pulse is managed as a tachycardia (synchronized cardioversion if unstable, drugs if stable). E describes the full arrest picture - pulseless, unresponsive and not breathing normally - which is how BLS recognises arrest.

  • A, B: a pulse is present, so this is not an arrest and not an indication for defibrillation.
  • C, D: both describe pulselessness, which is itself the shock indication; E is keyed as the most complete statement (see flag).

flags.title: Extraction damage and overlapping options
flags.html: Option C reads 'Pulseness' - almost certainly 'Pulselessness' with letters lost in extraction. Read that way, C, D and E all describe pulseless VT, which is shockable in each case; the key picks the fullest description.

hippo-t2c-em-Q27:
From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5), its cardiac arrest algorithm. This asks for the false statement. Cardioversion is synchronized to the QRS so the shock avoids the vulnerable T wave, whereas defibrillation delivers current at a random moment (the electrical cardioversion reference note), so A is false.

  • B: true - defibrillation is unsynchronized, for VF/pulseless VT where there is no organised QRS to sync to.
  • C: true - an unsynchronized shock in an organised rhythm can land on the T wave and induce VF; stable AF gets drugs (stable → drugs).
  • D: true - defibrillation uses high energy (for example 200 J biphasic).
  • E: true - the lecture's tachycardia algorithm sends unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse to synchronized cardioversion.

hippo-t2c-em-Q28.html:
The BLS algorithm opens with scene safety: a rescuer who becomes a second casualty (surf, traffic, electricity) helps no one, so C comes before touching the patient.

  • B: checking responsiveness is the second step, once the scene is safe.
  • A: the pulse check comes after shouting for help, and is limited to no more than 10 seconds together with a breathing check.
  • D: an AED is fetched (ideally by someone else) after activating the emergency response.
  • E: CPR starts once the patient is confirmed unresponsive, not breathing normally and pulseless.

flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

hippo-t2c-em-Q29.html:
In crisis resource management the leader stands back from hands-on tasks to keep the overview: they assign roles and tasks (E), prioritise, and keep the team working to one shared plan.

  • A: the leader has final say but invites input; making every decision alone breeds fixation errors.
  • B, C: 'independently' is the flaw - searching for the cause and working toward ROSC are team efforts the leader coordinates, not solo tasks.
  • D: the opposite - the leader should voice their mental model out loud so the team can follow and challenge it.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

hippo-t2c-em-Q30.html:
Crisis resource management is a bundle of team behaviours - know the environment, call for help early, avoid fixation, share the mental model, distribute workload - but the two that hold the rest together are effective leadership (someone owns the plan and assigns roles) and closed-loop communication (an order is directed at a named person, repeated back and confirmed done). So A.

  • B, C, D, E: each names genuine CRM principles, but they are supporting elements that depend on leadership and closed-loop communication to work; the key treats A as the pair that matters most.

hippo-t2c-em-Q31.html:
From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5), its cardiac arrest algorithm. The algorithm splits on rhythm: VF or pulseless VT is shocked, anything not shockable (asystole, PEA) goes straight back to CPR, with epinephrine every 3-5 min. The key implies the strip showed a non-shockable rhythm, so the next step is high-quality compressions, and with no advanced airway the ratio is 30:2 (D).

  • B: shocking asystole or PEA does nothing - compare Q32, the same stem with a shockable strip.
  • A, C: IV access and drugs are added once compressions are running, never in place of them.
  • E: continuous compressions with a breath every 6 seconds is for a patient with an advanced airway.

flags.title: The rhythm strip is missing
flags.html: The stem refers to a monitor strip that did not survive extraction from HippoNotes, so the rhythm cannot be checked here. The key only makes sense if it was non-shockable (asystole or PEA). Treat the explanation as conditional on that.

hippo-t2c-em-Q32.html:
From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5), its cardiac arrest algorithm. This is the same scenario as Q31 with a different strip: the key implies a shockable rhythm (VF or pulseless VT), and the algorithm's rule for those is a shock as soon as the defibrillator is on, then straight back to CPR for 2 minutes (B). Every minute of delay to the first shock lowers survival.

  • D: 30:2 CPR continues around the shock but must not delay it once the monitor shows VF/pVT.
  • A, C: IV access and epinephrine/amiodarone come after the first shocks.
  • E: a breath every 6 seconds is for a patient with an advanced airway, which he does not have.

flags.title: The rhythm strip is missing
flags.html: The stem refers to a monitor strip that did not survive extraction from HippoNotes, so the rhythm cannot be checked here. The key only makes sense if it was VF or pulseless VT. Treat the explanation as conditional on that.

hippo-t2c-em-Q33.html:
From 04 - Tachycardia: SVT and VT (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5). The keyed answer, VT, is a regular, wide-complex tachycardia - the lecture's rule is that a wide QRS tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise - with uniform, repeating broad complexes (monomorphic).

  • A, C: VF is chaotic, irregular deflections with no identifiable QRS complexes - coarse or fine by amplitude.
  • D: asystole is a flat line.
  • E: PEA is any organised rhythm without a pulse; it cannot be named from a strip alone, because the diagnosis is the missing pulse.

flags.title: The rhythm strip is missing
flags.html: The stem refers to a monitor strip that did not survive extraction from HippoNotes, so the rhythm cannot be checked against the key; the features above are what a VT strip should show. Treat the explanation as conditional on that.

hippo-t2c-em-Q34.html:
From 06 - Antiarrhythmic Therapies (PoM 1 Cardiology, Week 5), its cardiac arrest algorithm. A pulseless, unresponsive patient is in cardiac arrest, and the key implies a non-shockable rhythm - since option B (asystole) is not keyed, most likely an organised rhythm without a pulse, i.e. PEA. The non-shockable arm of the algorithm is CPR plus epinephrine as soon as possible, then every 3-5 min, while searching for reversible causes (Hs and Ts), so E.

  • D: PEA and asystole are not shockable; defibrillation is only for VF/pulseless VT.
  • B: presumably excluded by the strip showing electrical activity.
  • A, C: a pulseless patient is never malingering, and nothing points to opioids; an overdose would still be managed as an arrest.
